title: Flow Autoencoders are Effective Protein Tokenizers
claim: A discrete token codebook, learned or autoregressively generated, conditions a flow-matching decoder that turns noise into structured data.
layout: Left-to-right, tokens on left feeding a three-stage noise-to-structure flow, labeled velocity box
description: A single wide schematic with a purple palette. At left, two rows of color-graded token cells are labeled with the steps '(1) Discrete codebook conditions a flow model' and '(2) Autoregressively generate conditioning tokens'. The top row is a 'Learned codebook' strip. A downward arrow leads to a shorter token strip, which feeds a gray box holding ĉ. The second step shows a token strip fading in left to right under an arrow. Both token paths merge through a bracketed black line into the main flow. A gray box shows the velocity field v_θ(x_t, t, ĉ), with an arrow pointing right. Below it, a noisy point cloud of purple dots transitions through curved gray flow arrows into a partially formed cloud, then into a finished ribbon-style protein structure at right. The eye goes first to the protein and the point clouds.
caption: Schematic overview of our approach. (1) A learned discrete codebook conditions a flow matching model to reconstruct proteins using a diffusion loss. (2) The learned tokens can be used for downstream autoregressive generation, and the generated tokens condition the diffusion decoder to generate protein backbones.
abstract: Protein structure tokenizers enable the creation of multimodal models of protein structure, sequence, and function. Current approaches to protein structure tokenization rely on bespoke components that are invariant to spatial symmetries, but that are challenging to optimize and scale. We present Kanzi, a flow-based tokenizer for tokenization and generation of protein structures. Kanzi consists of a diffusion autoencoder trained with a flow matching loss. We show that this approach simplifies several aspects of protein structure tokenizers: frame-based representations can be replaced with global coordinates, complex losses are replaced with a single flow matching loss, and SE(3)-invariant attention operations can be replaced with standard attention. We find that these changes stabilize the training of parameter-efficient models that outperform existing tokenizers on reconstruction metrics at a fraction of the model size and training cost. An autoregressive model trained with Kanzi outperforms similar generative models that operate over tokens, although it does not yet match the performance of state-of-the-art continuous diffusion models. Code is available here: https://github.com/rdilip/kanzi/.
